title: Python Interview Practice — Iterators & Functional Built-ins
topics: Adds a counter to an iterable and returns index-value pairs.
Useful when a loop needs both the position and the item.

for i, value in enumerate(['a','b']):
    print(i, value)
Combines elements from multiple iterables position by position.
Useful for processing related lists together.

for name, mark in zip(names, marks):
    print(name, mark)
Applies a function to every item in an iterable and returns a map iterator.
Keeps elements for which a function returns a truthy value.
Useful for selecting elements that satisfy a condition.
Returns a new sorted list from an iterable.
Useful when the original iterable should remain unchanged.
Returns an iterator that accesses a sequence in reverse order.
Useful for reverse traversal without changing the original sequence.
any() checks whether at least one item is truthy; all() checks whether every item is truthy.
Useful for compact validation and condition checks.

any(x > 10 for x in nums)
all(x > 0 for x in nums)
key= tells these functions which derived value should control comparison.
Useful for sorting or finding records by a field such as length, age, or score.
iter() creates an iterator; next() retrieves its next item.
Useful for understanding iteration internals and implementing custom iteration.
Combines iteration tools with functions, collections, exceptions and interview-style reasoning.
Interviewers often test output prediction, lazy evaluation, edge cases and complexity.

topicQuestions.question: Which tool lazily pairs each element with its index without building a full list first?

topicQuestions.question: Which expression finds the first even number in a list without scanning further than necessary?
options: next(x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0)
[x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0][0]
hints: A generator expression produces values lazily, one at a time.
next() pulls just the first value that satisfies the condition.
This avoids building the full filtered list, unlike a list comprehension.

topicQuestions.question: What is the key difference between a generator expression and a list comprehension?
topicQuestions.code:
gen = (x for x in range(1000000))
lst = [x for x in range(1000000)]
options: Generators produce items lazily one at a time, using far less memory
They always produce different final values
Generators can only be used once inside a for loop
hints: Both can look almost identical, just with () vs [].
One materializes every value immediately into memory.
The generator expression yields values on demand, which is far more memory-efficient for large ranges.
